messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Javier has spent his entire career creating safe spaces for others. As a social ministry worker, he counsels the homeless, connects families with resources, and offers a calm presence in the midst of chaos. For the last six months, however, his own world has felt anything but safe. The finalization of his divorce from his partner, Marco, was supposed to be a relief, but it has only solidified a profound sense of isolation and fear that began on one specific night. That evening, an argument had escalated in a way it never had before. The sharp smell of whiskey on Marco’s breath filled their small apartment as his voice grew louder, culminating in the deafening slam of their bedroom door. Javier remembers being pushed to the floor, the rough texture of the rug against his cheek, and the terrifying weight of Marco holding him down, his arms pinned, unable to move or even breathe properly.

The memory of that night is not a distant story he tells himself; it is a landscape he is forced to revisit. It returns with a startling clarity, the images so vivid he can almost feel the pressure on his chest again. Sometimes, it is the sounds that ambush him—Marco's slurred, angry words echoing in his head as if he were right there in the room. When these memories surface, they bring with them a wave of overwhelming grief, not for the lost love, but for the loss of his own belief in his safety and judgment. The vividness of these recollections has made the world feel treacherous, sensitizing him to any reminder of that night. A memory of being restrained can make a friendly hand on his shoulder feel like an imminent attack, turning a simple gesture into a potent trigger.

His life is now governed by a constant, humming sense of threat. He startles violently at any unexpected movement in his periphery, a flinch he tries to hide from his colleagues at the community center. Night is the worst; the darkness seems to amplify every sound, and he finds it impossible to feel secure. This pervasive feeling of danger has driven him to adopt a series of rigid, exhausting routines. He checks the locks on his new apartment’s doors and windows repeatedly before bed, a ritual that offers only fleeting reassurance. The constant state of vigilance seems to keep the trauma fresh in his mind, ensuring the memories remain sharp and easily accessible, as if his brain is refusing to let its guard down. It has also made him acutely attuned to his triggers, turning his environment into a minefield of potential threats.

These triggers now dictate the boundaries of his shrinking world. The sound of a door slamming shut—a common occurrence at the busy ministry—instantly sends a jolt of panic through him, making him feel trapped and endangered. That sudden noise often brings back a fragment of the memory, the sound of his own bedroom door closing off his escape. In response to these moments, he has learned to freeze completely, a deer-in-headlights stillness that can last for several seconds. He also meticulously avoids the entire neighborhood where he and Marco used to live, even though it means cutting himself off from friends and familiar places. He had hoped that this avoidance, along with his fierce attempts to control and suppress any show of emotion, would keep the memories at bay. Instead, these strategies seem to have backfired; by treating the memories as threats to be contained, they have only gained power, ambushing him with greater intensity when his guard is down. His efforts to maintain a calm exterior only seem to make him more susceptible to being triggered by a sudden sound or the smell of alcohol on a client’s breath.

The cycle has become self-sustaining. A trigger, like the smell of alcohol during a counseling session, activates his sense of immediate threat and brings the memory rushing back. His feeling of being in danger compels him to retreat, to lock his doors, to avoid. This avoidance, in turn, makes the outside world seem even more menacing and his triggers more powerful. He came to therapy last week after an incident at work. A man he was counseling, distraught and smelling of beer, had reached out and grabbed his arm to steady himself. Javier froze, his breath catching in his throat, unable to speak or move. The man, confused and concerned by his reaction, had backed away. In that moment, Javier realized his own trauma was now a barrier to the work that once gave his life meaning. He is terrified that he is permanently broken, but he holds onto the hope that he might one day feel safe enough in his own skin to help others feel safe in theirs.
